newsitem.title: USA: Talks to resume ahead of UPS strike deadline.
newsitem.headline: Talks to resume ahead of UPS strike deadline.

text.p: Talks aimed at averting a strike will resume on Sunday between the International Brotherhood of Teamsters and United Parcel Service, the biggest U.S. shipper, a federal mediator said.
"We are going into this negotiating session with a real sense of urgency," said John Calhoun Wells, director of the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service.

He said Ron Carey, president of the Teamsters, had vowed not to extend again the deadline for a strike against UPS, set for midnight EDT (0400 on Monday GMT). The union postponed an original strike deadline on Thursday at Wells' request.

"He (Carey) has told me unequivocally this is a drop-dead deadline," Wells said outside headquarters of the mediation service where the talks were to resume at 6 p.m. EDT (2200 GMT), six hours before the strike was to begin.

Wells said a strike would adversely affect "a lot" of Americans. Atlanta-based UPS employs 301,000 people in the United States, 185,000 of whom are represented by the Teamsters, including package sorters, loaders and drivers.
With its trademark shiny brown trucks, UPS normally handles about 12 million packages a day, an estimated four-fifths of the ones shipped by ground nationwide.
The company said last week that the threat of a strike was costing it about $5 million a day in business lost to competitors such as the U.S. Postal Service and Federal Express Corp.
Wells said the two sides remained apart on a number of issues, but declined to elaborate.
On Saturday the Teamsters made what they described as slight changes in their latest offer based on 15 hours of bargaining last week overseen by federal mediators.

About 60 percent of UPS workers are part-timers, according to the union, which wants the company to provide thousands of new full-time job openings. The company has offered to create 1,000 new full-time jobs from part-time positions over the life of a proposed five-year contract.
The union and UPS also remain at odds on curbing the company's ability to subcontract jobs, strengthening pension benefits and boosting health and safety standards.

In what it called its "last, best and final" contract offer on Thursday, the company offered to boost pay for both full- and part-time workers by $1.50 to $2.50 per hour over five years. Under the company proposal, a profit-sharing plan would provide a first payment of $3,060 to full-time employees and $1,530 to part-time workers in 1997.
The last round of bargaining recessed on Friday night.
With revenue of $22.4 billion in 1996, UPS annually handles about three billion parcels and documents, shipped to more than 200 countries from 1,700 hubs and centres.
